core: Multiple properties or communities under management
Portfolio or regional leadership layers, not single-site operators
Organizations growing through acquisition, expansion, or leadership change
howTheyActuallyBuy: Most active business today is mid-market, even though the aspirational target is a portfolio-scale executive buyer.
Many large operators buy decentrally — property by property or region by region. A single large logo can behave like a collection of independent buyers.
The buying committee varies by account: some centralize, others decide independently at each property with little connection between locations.
buyingStructureNote: Organizational buying structure — centralized versus decentralized — is as important a segmentation lens as portfolio size. Treating every large account as one enterprise decision misses how expansion actually happens.
fitSignals: Can see performance issues but struggle to prioritize what to act on
Relies on individual judgment rather than a shared standard — an experienced manager and a new one make different calls on identical data
Inconsistent execution and outcomes across properties
Increasing friction as the portfolio scales
Already runs a PMS with adjacent, often free, functionality — the value case has to clear a real bar

segments.name: Compliance & Workforce Readiness
who: Multi-state operators with regulatory exposure (Fair Housing, ADA, state-specific)
Portfolios with high front-line turnover where consistent onboarding matters
Property managers facing audit cycles or reputational risk events
theySay: We have inconsistent training across sites and we're a lawsuit waiting to happen
Our policies are outdated; we don't know what's actually getting enforced
We have no way to verify our properties are operating to standard
segments.basic: Codified policy content and a system of record for course completion — close to commodity as adjacent systems build similar functionality in for free.
segments.differentiated: Verification in the field, consistency benchmarked across properties, and recommended corrective action when standards slip.
segments.fit: Strong propensity to buy when pain becomes acute. Regulatory and liability exposure is urgency-driven — lead with value positioning, not feature comparison.

segments.name: Resident Growth & Retention
who: Lease-up communities and value-add renovations needing tour velocity
theySay: Our occupancy is behind submarket and we don't know why
Negative reviews are killing tour-to-lease conversion and we're reactive
Renewal rates are dropping but we hear nothing until move-out
segments.fit: Active strategic question rather than settled. These capabilities primarily serve prospect acquisition — a different buyer and funnel stage from the retention story anchoring the rest of the platform.

segments.name: Workforce Performance
who: Operators with frontline turnover above industry median
Companies investing in maintenance and skilled-trades upskilling
Multi-site portfolios where employee experience varies widely
HR leaders building the case for retention investment
theySay: It takes months to get a new hire productive and we lose them just as fast
Our maintenance techs lack the certifications we need to scale service hours
Engagement scores are dropping and we don't know which sites are struggling
segments.basic: Course count and portfolio size — this does not reflect the real value delivered.
segments.differentiated: Connecting training content to performance and engagement outcomes: recommending what to assign, to whom, and showing whether it worked.
segments.fit: The clearest example of the value philosophy in practice.

segments.name: Enterprise & Multi-Stakeholder Portfolios
who: Large portfolios with multi-stakeholder buying committees
Organizations looking for a strategic partner, not a vendor
Accounts with a foothold in one property but no broader relationship
segments.fit: Buying structure is more predictive than unit count. Growth is often less about expanding one agreement and more about earning a second, independent buying decision at the next property.

valueModel.what: The individual solutions that generate activity and performance data — training, surveys, policy, field verification, resident marketing, reputation.
Benchmarks across properties and surfaces priorities and trends.
Recommends what to do next. The clearest, most defensible differentiator.

basicVsDifferentiated.basic: Functionality the market already expects, often free or cheap elsewhere — course libraries, completion tracking, basic survey distribution. Necessary for credibility, weak ground for premium value.
basicVsDifferentiated.differentiated: Functionality that connects across products, benchmarks performance, or recommends action. Where the defensible value sits.

realCompetitiveThreat: There is no direct full-platform competitor today. The more immediate threat is property management systems bundling adjacent functionality — like basic training — into their platform for free, potentially displacing point-solution categories entirely. Those systems record activity but don't connect it or recommend action, which is exactly why the action layer is the least-replicable differentiator.

marketContext.detail: Average portfolio size across accounts with data on file.
Accounts with 25,000+ units — a small, high-value tier.
New-logo win rate, varying by product and historically lower.
Expansion win rate within existing accounts — expansion converts substantially better than new logo.

expansionNote: Expansion deals within existing mid-market accounts are the single largest source of deal volume in the business today.
